Two-thirds of the companies on the Forbes AI 50 list now use some form of usage-based pricing, reflecting AI’s variable costs and unpredictable demand. At the second annual Monetize conference last month, Metronome CEO and Cofounder Scott Woody put it more bluntly: today’s leading companies operate in ways that would seem “alien” to traditional SaaS businesses. These companies are iterating much faster on pricing, prioritizing market share over ARR, and pursuing multiple go-to-market strategies at once.

More than 300 leaders from fast-moving companies like Replit, Fin, Snowflake, and Clay came together at Monetize to trade notes on pricing, cost management, and scaling AI products as customer expectations change. Across sessions, five approaches for how companies are now approaching the economics of AI monetization came up repeatedly.

Hybrid pricing: Packaging usage with subscriptions and credits

A year ago, it was common to expect usage-based pricing to displace subscriptions. Businesses are still using them, just in a new way.We’re seeing more companies using subscriptions to package up variable usage, often through credits.

Aisling O’Reilly, Fin’s director of product for monetization, described the evolution of her own company’s pricing models. The company evolved from a platform subscription to a hybrid model, introducing outcome-based pricing when it launched Fin AI Agent. Initially, customers paid for each support conversation resolved by the agent. As the product expanded into actions like recommending products, qualifying leads, and booking meetings, its original (and only) billable metric became an insufficient representation of customer value. Fin introduced additional billable outcomes, letting customers choose the outcome they wanted from each conversation type and pay based on its value. Customers can commit to a pool of credits, then draw down against that pool across outcomes without having to forecast each one separately.

What’s emerging for Fin and many other companies is a layered model, with subscriptions for actions and predictability, usage-based pricing for agentic work, and credits to simplify multiple usage or outcome units.

Predictability is becoming a product feature

One of the biggest challenges with usage-based billing is giving customers more predictable costs. They need to understand what drives usage, anticipate spend, set spend limits, and connect usage to value. Many companies have addressed those requirements through in-product dashboards, predictions, and other types of tooling.

Snowflake Senior Director Ryan Campbell explained how he and his team help customers monitor and control their consumption through in-product tooling like forecasting, calculators, scenario builders, and usage visibility. Similarly, Stripe’s Head of Global Pricing and Commercialization, Sam Lee, described the usage control pane, where users can see alerts, set and adjust spending controls, and manage consumption, as a new standard.

Commercial terms can also offer more predictability while keeping charges tied to usage. Annual usage buckets, discounted overages, and first-year fixed contracts with follow-on true-ups all offer customers clearer controls to manage variable bills.

As bills become more unpredictable, strong usage controls become part of what customers are paying for. Those controls help build trust in both the company and the product.

Falling AI costs and rising usage call for flexible packaging

With advances in AI, companies are able to package the same product in different ways. Subscriptions can house lower-cost and rate-limited experiences, while usage-based billing can be used for more resource-intensive agent work. Replit uses both as model costs and agent workloads shift, said Michele Catasta, the company’s president and head of AI.

When Replit’s agents used to run for just a few minutes, the company charged 25¢ per agent checkpoint. But as runtimes grew, some jobs cost Replit several dollars while users still paid just 25¢. The company adopted usage-based billing to close the gap, aligning prices more closely with the amount of work performed by its agents.

This move solved one problem and introduced another: unpredictable spending and abrupt paywalls for users accustomed to a straightforward monthly subscription. As inference costs fell—due in part to increasingly capable open-source models and the pressure they put on frontier-model prices—Replit introduced a rate-limited Free Mode. This gives users the ability to keep building on a simple subscription. The company changes elements of its pricing several times a month, passing savings on to customers.

This opens up more flexible packaging beyond the one-product, one-pricing-model approach. Companies can combine subscriptions and usage-based billing, then adjust the mix as the underlying economics shift. That lets them offer versions of the same product at different speeds, prices, and service levels.

Finance’s new mandate: Proving AI value

While tokens might determine a company’s costs, it’s rare that they represent the value customers think they’re buying. In a session on how finance teams can measure AI’s value, Karan Parekh, Clay’s head of finance, said the company doesn’t want to be in the business of “upcharging and taxing tokens.” When pricing, Clay treats model tokens and third-party data as pass-through inputs, separate from the differentiated value its product provides.

Clay applies the same approach to evaluate its own internal AI investments. The sales team tracks productivity, the product team focuses on development time, and support teams measure throughput and customer satisfaction. Parekh’s team is comfortable with its own AI spending growing faster than revenue only if it’s producing something distinctive Clay couldn’t otherwise achieve.

Attribution is difficult when multiple tools and workflow changes contribute to the same result, making token-level ROI calculations misleading. Clay’s solution is to measure AI tooling against those function-specific targets, reviewing them quarterly to track whether those AI investments prove out. For finance teams, operational outcomes are a more useful lens than focusing on input costs.

Pricing information needs to be readable by both machines and humans

Agents are already influencing how products are discovered and evaluated, even if autonomous enterprise purchasing has yet to fully emerge.

To understand how buyers might encounter pricing in AI-generated answers, Kyle Poyar, founder of Growth Unhinged, tested how six AI engines presented pricing information for companies on the Cloud 100. He analyzed 7,600 AI-generated responses. For one unnamed company, negative pricing language appeared in 88% of responses. Without accessible pricing for this organization, LLMs resorted to scouring informal sources like Reddit and reported back prices ranging from $100–$2,400 per user, per month, a 24x difference.

Pricing information might be fully visible to humans who visit your site, but if it’s blocked from crawlers or rendered in a way agents can’t reliably interpret, it’s basically invisible. While autonomous enterprise procurement is still early, pricing now has two different audiences to serve. The person accountable for the purchase is still in the picture, but they’ve made room for the machine helping them evaluate the purchase.

AI monetization is becoming an adaptive system

AI products, model economics, and usage patterns are changing far too quickly for pricing to stay static. Across sessions, leaders described identifying what customers value, giving them more control over spending, and adjusting pricing and packaging as products and business economics change.

Watch the recorded sessions from Monetize 2026 for the full conversations with leaders from Replit, Fin, Snowflake, Clay, Growth Unhinged, and Stripe.

Today, we’re sharing three major improvements to support this broader set of needs. Link can now help agents complete more purchases with incremental authorization and guidance on how to overcome checkout obstacles; analyze consumer spending to make better product recommendations; and provide purchase protection if an agent makes a mistake.

Help agents complete more purchases

Online checkout flows are complex, and agents do not always have all the information they need at the start of a purchase. The final price may change because of taxes, shipping, or other costs added later in the process.

Link now supports incremental authorization, which lets agents request a higher approved amount when the final price exceeds the original. For example, a consumer might ask an agent to book a flight, then add a checked bag after approving the initial fare. With Link, the agent can update the approved amount to include the baggage fee instead of restarting the purchase and placing a second hold on the consumer’s card. This helps agents account for price changes and complete more purchases with less intervention.

When an agent encounters additional payment obstacles, Link provides specific guidance on how to proceed to increase the chances of a successful payment. For example, Link can provide a URL that the agent can send to the consumer to complete a 3D Secure challenge. Or if the original payment method was declined, the agent can ask the consumer to choose another and create a new spend request.

Many of the world’s leading fintechs use Stripe to build and scale, including 32 of the Forbes Fintech 50 (and counting). As these businesses expand into new markets, they need to deliver the same fast, reliable experience everywhere while supporting local payment methods, navigating local compliance requirements, and integrating new banking partners.

We’re introducing three updates to help fintechs launch products and grow internationally more easily: simpler payout management with Stripe Global Payouts, support for stablecoin cards in more countries, and unified APIs for building global financial products.

Here’s what’s new.

Send payouts to recipients in more than 160 markets

We’ve expanded Global Payouts to more markets and made it easier to set up and manage. Businesses can now send instant stablecoin payouts to recipients in 160 markets and traditional currency payouts to recipients in more than 100, directly from the Stripe Dashboard.

Fintechs can also use Global Payouts programmatically—by embedding hosted forms or integrating with flexible APIs—to enable use cases like loan disbursements, remittances, investment withdrawals, and neobank cash-outs within their products. Issue stablecoin cards in more countries

Stripe Treasury allows businesses to settle Stripe earnings, hold funds, convert currencies, spend with cards, and send outbound payments. Fintechs can also bring these same capabilities to their customers by embedding financial tools and services using Stripe Treasury for platforms.

Stripe Treasury, Global Payouts, and Issuing are all part of Stripe’s unified stack for fintechs, meaning they easily integrate with one another and KYC information can be shared, reducing compliance work and additional user verification steps. Many businesses on Stripe use Stripe data to power their applications. A subscription business relies on current plan data to update a customer’s account or grant access to paid features; an ecommerce company uses payment confirmation data to fulfill an order.

As agents take on more tasks and businesses build more customer-facing workflows around Stripe data, applications need data they can act on immediately. Businesses on Stripe have asked us for an easier way to keep their application databases current. Developers have typically done this themselves by repeatedly calling Stripe APIs or building webhook infrastructure that copies changes into their databases. They then have to monitor the integration, handle failed or out-of-order events, and regularly check that all their stored data still matches Stripe.

To keep databases current without requiring developers to build and maintain custom integrations, we’re launching real-time sync to Postgres through Stripe Data Pipeline. You can sync payment, customer, subscription, and other Stripe data to a Postgres database that powers your applications. Stripe handles the sync end to end.

Sync Stripe data directly to Postgres

Data Pipeline already lets businesses send Stripe data to a data warehouse or cloud storage for analytics and reporting. Anthropic uses it to accelerate month-end reconciliation, Cursor uses it to report on revenue and churn, and Lime uses it to automate financial reporting.

The new real-time sync sends Stripe data directly to Postgres databases, including those hosted by Supabase, AWS, Neon, Databricks Lakebase, and other providers. To set up a sync, connect your Postgres database and select the Stripe tables you need. Data Pipeline backfills those tables and keeps them synchronized as the source data changes in Stripe. No code is required.

“The value that real-time sync to Postgres creates replaces all of the other work we had to do to get our data,” said Josh Siegel, CPO and CTO at Company Sage. “It’s much easier for us to reduce our old API and webhook infrastructure and just use Stripe Data Pipeline instead.”

Keep data current automatically

Once you set up the sync, Data Pipeline copies existing data from the selected Stripe tables into your connected Postgres database. As data changes in Stripe, Data Pipeline delivers updates to Postgres in seconds.

Data Pipeline regularly audits the synchronized records against the source data in Stripe and resolves discrepancies. The result is a reliable, real-time copy of Stripe data in Postgres, and one fewer system for developers to build, monitor, and debug.

Get started

Postgres is the first Data Pipeline destination to support real-time syncing of Stripe data. Support for Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Amazon Redshift, Databricks, and cloud storage platforms is coming soon.

Real-time sync to Postgres is available in public preview and free to get started. Create a pipeline in the Stripe Dashboard, or read our docs to learn more.

https://stripe.com/blog/where-pricing-is.cuerpo:
Token billing is useful infrastructure and, for almost every company, a bad customer-facing pricing model. In its simplest form, passthrough pricing charges customers for the model tokens their usage consumes, plus a markup on the underlying cost. If you’re building your pricing around that token consumption, you’re letting your costs determine your price.

That’s reflected in how our customers are using token billing today. They need it on the backend to track usage, manage markups, and protect their unit economics, but they don’t want those details defining how they price their product.

This gets at something I’ve been saying for a while: your invoice should be where you define your value to your customer.

Token-based billing has an invoice problem

This raises the obvious question: why did we build token billing in the first place? Because it’s a safeguard against runaway compute costs, and it’s easy to deploy and explain. For model providers, token usage is the product. For most other AI companies, token billing can be a useful place to start: tokens provide an obvious, countable basis for pricing. But neither subscription seats nor tokens accurately reflect the value your customer receives.

Token billing positions your product as a commodity markup on top of an actual commodity. It shows the customer an accounting of which models were used, how many tokens were consumed, and what markup was applied. But presenting your model mix, input costs, and margins to a customer misses the point. If their invoice shows that you used 10 models with a 10% markup on one, 5% on another, and 25% on another, you’ve defined your value as the difference between your price and somebody else’s model costs.

As those models become cheaper and more interchangeable, customers can challenge your markup or route around you entirely. Competition drives the markup, and potentially your business, toward zero.

A better model: Unified credits

Many of our customers are already using Metronome as a margin-tuning system, not just to deploy pricing models. They make model-routing decisions upstream, then send the resulting token usage to Metronome—either broken out by customer or attributed to a single aggregate customer for cost tracking. Our product then gives them visibility into token consumption so they can manage costs and tune their margins.

That gives companies control over their internal economics, but it doesn’t solve the invoice problem. They still need a presentation layer on top of the core modeling that translates the underlying usage into something tangible for customers. More companies are turning to a unified credit model.

A unified credit model creates a credit-based burndown. Customers draw down a common credit balance as they use different product operations, with each task consuming credits at its own rate based on the underlying token consumption. One operation might enrich a dataset, another might generate an image. In that case, the invoice can show the customer those enrichments or generated images, not the 10 models you used in the process and the markup applied to each.

The point isn’t to eliminate complexity; it’s to keep it behind the scenes. Metronome preserves token-level metering, so companies can continue routing models upstream and tuning for margin and performance as workloads change or new models are introduced. But with a unified credit model, your customer doesn’t have to parse all that complexity. On their invoice, the customer sees credits tied to the work the product performs, not tokens tied to the model costs.

Why output-based pricing is the ideal (and outcome-based pricing is a myth)

Unified credits are a stepping stone to output-based pricing, which is the best way to align AI consumption pricing with value today.

There are three common pricing metrics in AI. The first is an input, which is a cost, like a token.

The second is an outcome, which could mean the customer making more money, building more pipeline, or reducing churn. Outcomes can help you orient your product around customer value, but they’re difficult to turn into defensible pricing metrics.

Outcome-based pricing only works in a very limited set of circumstances and is largely a luxury reserved for the corporate super-rich. You either need monopoly-like power—enough control over the transaction and its underlying telemetry to measure the outcome, and enough market power to make customers accept that pricing—or a very high ticket price, since only very large contracts can justify the investment required to measure outcomes. At a high enough ticket price, you can afford to instrument a workflow end-to-end and prove mathematically that you’ve made it much more efficient: it requires fewer people, work gets done faster, or inventory turns more quickly. Every quarter, you can prove that value back to the customer and charge a fee as a function of that outcome.

For everyone else, outcome-based pricing is, for all intents and purposes, a myth. There’s a telemetry gap around what counts as the outcome, whether it occurred, and whether your product caused it.

Say, for example, I sell you a sales agent and charge you based on the revenue it generates. I’ve immediately invited a dispute over the relative value of human labor versus automated labor. Did the agent generate the sale or was it the sales rep? Was it marketing? Would the customer have purchased anyway? The outcome might be valuable, but it can’t be objectively attributed to the product.

The third way to price is on outputs.An output is an objective, verifiable metric, like generating an image or sending an email. Fin’s pricing, based on resolved support conversations, is considered the poster child for outcome-based pricing. I would argue it’s actually an output. The outcome of customer support is happy customers; a resolved support ticket is something you can objectively count.

All companies should do the same: define your output metric, call it an outcome, and convince the market that you’re right.

Where pricing is headed

Pricing models are slow to change because customers compare you with the rest of your competition. There’s a heavy penalty for departing from the herd.

But once a new model takes hold, the market can change very quickly. It’s Darwinian: a pricing model can look completely maladaptive, then suddenly become adaptive and spread through the category.

Three years ago, our team at Metronome predicted that hybrid pricing—some combination of seats plus usage—would become a prominent business model. We built support for it, and it went largely unused by our customers for around 18 months. Then, as of August 2026, roughly one in six (and growing) Stripe users that had crossed key revenue milestones were actively using or rolling out hybrid pricing. The model we’d been hypothesizing about for years seemed to catch on all at once.

Fin followed a similar pattern. Three years ago, almost no one in the AI customer-support category was talking about outcome-based pricing. Within a quarter of Fin introducing pricing based on resolved support conversations, all five of the leading companies in the category had committed to some version of outcome-based pricing.

Nothing changed, then everything changed. Once the product category and its buyers reached a certain level of maturity, the preference cascaded through the market.

As agents become more involved in both buying services and doing work, I suspect we’ll see the same thing with output-based pricing.

Subscription and seat-based pricing have been dominant thus far partly because they’re straightforward for humans to understand and compare. It’s easy to explain a fixed price per month or a fixed price per user to human buyers. An agent, on the other hand, can account for far more variables and match the price of each task more closely to its value.

One analogy for this trajectory is high-frequency trading. Trading algorithms operate at a level of speed and complexity that humans can’t. Something similar could happen with pricing. As agents increasingly evaluate and purchase services, pricing models won’t be limited by how much complexity a human buyer can handle. Agents also make the work itself easier to measure. Each task leaves an audit trail, which makes more activities observable and verifiable without a separate monitoring system.

As more work moves through agents, I expect the measurable outputs they produce to become pricing metrics—even if they’re still often marketed as outcomes.

El Fuenlabrada, como el Palmer, también se fue de vacío de Sevilla, derrotado por un equipo que pica piedra, muerde y se siente cómodo en registros anotadores moderados. Dos triunfos en tres jornadas acumula este Caja 87 que ha interiorizado lo que tiene que hacer y lo ha llevado a la práctica con espartana disciplina sobreponiéndose, no se olvide esto, a la ausencia seguramente de su mejor anotador, Moody, lesionado. En un partido durísimo, de alta tensión e igualdad extrema hasta el final, el Caja 87 se esmeró en dos defensas sobresalientes sobre Benite que dejaron el triunfo en casa y desencadenaron la felicidad en los más de cinco mil seguidores que se dieron cita en San Pablo.

Mendikote sí horadó la canasta fuenlabreña, igual que Webster, pero su tiro se ejecutó fuera de tiempo. Un triple de Iván Cruz y y dos tiros libres de Mateo Díaz daban las primeras ventajas al Fuenlabrada (9-12) en un partido marcado por la igualdad, sin síntomas entonces de que pudiera romperse pronto. Juani Díez cambió pronto a todo el quinteto y Rafa García, que juega con máscara, restablecía la igualdad con un fantástico dos más uno en aro pasado.

Realmente estaba tomando buenos lanzamientos el Caja 87, pero la eficacia brillaba por entonces por su ausencia. Al 12-18 visitante replicaron los cajistas con un triple de Webster, que a veces produce poco en relación con todo el balón que absorbe. Entonces, Nacho Varela entró en ignición con un serial de once puntos consecutivos, nueve de ellos facturados desde el triple (39-36). Que el equipo da la cara, cree en lo que hace y rara vez se desconecta completamente, resulta innegable. Lo ha demostrado sobre todo en San Pablo, donde ha ganado dos encuentros y ha perdido uno, ante un candidato al ascenso y en el tiempo extra tras ponerlo contra las cuerdas.

Fuera de casa, sin embargo, aún no ha vencido y este sábado dispone de su tercera oportunidad para quebrar esa tendencia. Cayó en Madrid, contra el Estudiantes; también lo hizo en Córdoba, en la última jugada del partido; y ahora se presenta en Menorca, donde lo recibe un rival con el cuchillo entre los dientes y mucho más necesitado, casi en una situación límite. Ninguno de sus cinco partidos ha ganado el conjunto balear, que la temporada pasada se clasificó para el play off y este verano transformó su plantilla. Se pensó que estaría entre los candidatos al ascenso. Y aún está a tiempo porque de contrastados elementos dispone, pero la prioridad del Básquet Menorca pasa por sumar su primera victoria y dejar el farolillo rojo.

Entrenado por Javier Zamora, el equipo menorquín ha perdido con el Grupo Alega Cantabria (69-68), el HLA Alicante (64-81), el Palencia (91-76), el Fibwi Palma (67-72) y el Partizán de Fuenlabrada (90-76). A ese repóquer de derrotas hay que unir la encajada en la Copa contra el HLA Alicante (91-83). Del rival del Caja 87 llama la atención que apenas anote 70 puntos por encuentro y acierte un 25% de sus triples.

Se sospecha que en algún momento despertará y alguien pagará los platos rotos. Por esos, los niveles de alerta del Caja 87 deben ser máximos. No es un día para descuidarse en defensa sino para multiplicar esfuerzos y ayudas. El pívot Wildens Leveque, jugador franquicia del Cáceres la pasada temporada en Segunda FEB, lidera con 10 puntos y 11 rebotes de medias la estadística de este Menorca que también cuenta en su plantilla con Pol Figueras, Adams Sola y dos contrastados perimetrales que militaron en el Betis Baloncesto: Hansel Atencia y Cvetkovic. Ojo al serbio, que promedia 12 puntos con un 57% en el tiro exterior.

Por talento de sus jugadores y amplitud de plantilla, no se entiende que el Menorca cierre la tabla, pero es así y esto demuestra la dificultad de la Primera FEB, donde para equipos como el cajista no hay partidos cómodos ni llanuras en el calendario.

Priorizando la defensa, el Caja 87 necesita a nivel individual una mayor regularidad ofensiva de Webster y Moody, pero también que Nacho Varela afine en sus lanzamientos liberados y que Cecilia, cada vez mejor defendido, halle la manera de poner al servicio del equipo su versión más brillante. Con la suma de todos, cada uno en su rol, el conjunto hispalense está capacitado para competir en la cancha de un equipo a priori puntero que se juega su credibilidad en los dos próximos partidos.

Un rebote ofensivo de Mendikote transformaba la primera canasta cajista cuando ya se habían consumido dos minutos y medio de partido, pero el Covirán, muy activo en defensa, ensuciaba todos los ataques de su rival y se disparó hasta el 2-11 con triple de McGrew.

Varela conectaba bajo aro con Bolavie en un errático Caja 87 que necesitaba un esfuerzo extraordinario para anotar y se mostraba absolutamente cegado desde la línea del tiro libre. Apenas siete puntos, tras mate de Bolavie, acumulaba en siete minutos. Y afortunadamente seguía en partido porque el Covirán tampoco fue precisamente un dechado de finura en el tiro. Aun así, la concesión de triples liberados le permitió doblar en el marcador y escaparse hasta el 9-20 ante un apático y gripado Caja 87, muy apagado, entonces sobrepasado físicamente por un incómodo adversario que le aplicó el rodillo en el primer cuarto (11-23).

Soumbey-Alley al rescate

Muy lejos del nivel esperado, el Caja 87 necesitaba reaccionar buscando soluciones contra la asfixiante defensa del Covirán, que difícilmente concedía lanzamientos liberados. Ahí radicaba su fortaleza. Como, además, el Caja 87 no rentabilizaba sus visitas al 4,60, la remontada no se avistaba. Saliendo del banquillo, Soumbey-Alley abrió gas y aumentó las revoluciones de su equipo (17-23) ante un Granada empeñado en pegarle el hachazo al partido aplicando el veneno del tiro exterior.

Parcial de 6-0 y Soumbey-Alley, con la cinta en la cabeza, se multiplicaba, defendía con firmeza, reboteaba y asumía tiros, crecido. Subían la intensidad los anfitriones, o al menos lo intentaban, pero el Covirán aumentaba la distancia de seguridad y colocaba los 13 de ventaja tras triples de Kljajic, McGrew y técnica a Latorre (19-32). Sin Soumbey-Alley en la cancha, el Caja 87 no encontró un solo referente al que agarrarse más allá del ardor, la garra y el físico de Mendikote.

El público, disconforme con el arbitraje, la tomó con los jueces del partido, pero el verdadero problema radicaba en lo puramente baloncestístico. La diferencia era entonces abismal (21-35). El Covirán tenía completamente maniatado al Caja 87, que se estampaba contra la defensa granadina una y otra vez sin que pudiera poner en órbita a ninguno de sus estiletes ofensivos. En un ritmo pastoso y lento, de mucho contacto, con pocas transiciones y un viaje tras otro al 4,60, el Covirán Granada se sentía muy cómodo y acorazado, en el camino correcto (23-37).

En ese bloqueo persistente, el Caja 87 no se descompuso. Insistió con Nacho Varela a los mandos y cocinó un 6-0 (28-37) que Gauzin respondió con un 3+1 y falta de Webster (29-41). Bolavie falló otros dos tiros libres, pero luego el belga se redimió anotando bajo aro y confirmando, al descanso, que la suya era la más productiva vía anotadora de su equipo (31-41). En el ecuador, los sevillanos apenas habían facturado 8 de sus 17 tiros libres y uno de sus ocho lanzamientos triples. De capa caída estaba el ataque, negado por esa tupida y bien ajustada defensa visitante en la que se enredaron, sin saber cómo zafarse, los hombres de Juani Díez.

Giro tras el descanso

Varela bajaba de los diez al comienzo del tercer cuarto, y por dos veces, mediante sendos triples que precedieron a un mate atronador, bestial, de Bolavie, a una mano y por el carril central posterizando a Barro en la jugada más espectacular del partido (41-46). Soumbey-Alley, todo corazón y compromiso, se lanzó hasta dos veces al suelo jugándose el físico en busca de una pelota imposible y elevando la cota del esfuerzo del equipo. Transformó dos tiros libres de una falta flagrante (43-46) y se marchó al banco con una sentida y merecida ovación de la grada.

Microondas total, el togolés había cambiado el encuentro con su despliegue de energía mientras el Caja 87 seguía restando mediante el efectivo juego de pies de Ramón Vilà. Bolavie, desde el 4,60, completaba la remontada (50-49) y un parcial de 19-8 desde el descanso. Definitivamente se había reactivado el Caja 87, mucho más vivo, intenso y atento al rebote. Moody estrenaba su casillero de triples (55-52) y Cecilia ya empezaba a hacerse notar mientras Kljajic daba un paso al frente para liderar el ataque de su equipo con el partido en un pañuelo, absolutamente nivelado. Rafa García erraba lo 'infallable' en una penetración con extensión y Moody, con una 'bombita', dejaba el 59-60 al final del tercer periodo.

A la prórroga

Webster contestaba a Parham, pero Barro castigaba en una desaplicación defensiva (61-64) que no podía permitirse a esas alturas el Caja 87. Luego tiró el equipo un ataque a la basura tras consumir el tiempo sin sacar de fondo y otra vez la conexión entre Parham y Barro ponía en aprietos a los sevillanos (61-66), de nuevo enredados en la defensa nazarí, que había vuelto a subir su nivel. Ajustó hasta el 65-66 y malgastó varios lanzamientos exteriores para ponerse por delante. No era el día en el triple por más segundas opciones que apilara el equipo. Kljajic clavaba un triple psicológico, Bolavic se colgaba de nuevo y Barro se lo devolvía.

Dos faltas en ataque, de Soumbey-Alley y Bolavie, le cortaron el rollo al Caja 87, que a falta de dos minutos tenía a tiro de cuatro puntos a un resistente y tenaz Covirán que aguantaba cada embestida hispalense. Bolavie estaba en todas partes, qué despliegue más abrumador el suyo en los tableros. Restando 41 segundos, máximo suspense, problema técnico en la mesa y dos ataques cajistas que acaban en una falta de tres tiros para Moody que iguala el duelo tras fallar uno (73-73). Con 14 segundos se la jugó Parham, erró; y con nueve décimas, turno de Kljajic, cuyo falló condujo a esa prórroga que salió cruz para los verdirrojos.

Balance positivo de victorias en tres jornadas, pleno de alegrías en San Pablo, una defensa por momentos granítica, un funcionamiento coral y una personalidad en desarrollo que puede cuajar en algo no solo interesante sino también productivo y eficaz. Rentable. Que no se mueva ni ... un varal, empleando el argot cofrade, podría aquí subrayarse a cuenta del Caja 87 y su estreno en la Primera FEB, que hasta la fecha ha arrojado más noticias positivas que negativas. Pero el baloncesto no se detiene. La noria sigue girando. Cada fin de semana prepara un nuevo examen y el Caja 87, lejos de estancarse o conformarse con lo que ya ha hecho (nada en realidad), tiene que insistir en la misma idea de juego para perfeccionarla y seguir llenando de victorias el granero en pos del objetivo de la permanencia. Sin perder nunca la humildad, la propia del que tiene que hacerse un nombre en esta liga.

Esa primera meta volante, la salvación, es la única que cruzar obligatoriamente en su debut en la categoría. Queda un mundo. Y ya se sabe que un par de malos resultados lo cuestionan todo y, al revés, dos victorias encadenadas pueden llegar a sobrevalorar el conjunto de un equipo en proceso de construcción. Este sábado (18.30 horas, Baloncesto TV), el Insolac Caja 87 se examina en Córdoba, seguramente el escenario en el que más veces ha jugado, después de San Pablo, desde su fundación. En pretemporada lo hizo hasta en dos ocasiones: ganó al Coto en la fase previa de la Copa de Andalucía y se dio el lujazo de jugar la final del torneo regional en el pabellón Vista Alegre contra el Unicaja, para cuyo superior potencial no tuvo ya antídoto. Las diferencias entre un plantel potente de Liga Endesa y uno diseñado para salvarse con cierta holgura en la Primera FEB se hicieron patentes.

Esta tercera comparecencia será diferente. La competición oficial ha arrancado y ya no es tiempo de probaturas. Importa cada partido. El triunfo que se escapa ya no vuelve y perder contra un rival directo, como es el caso de este sábado, duele el doble. A diferencia del Caja 87, el Coto Córdoba suma una victoria y dos derrotas, pero ha disputado las dos últimas jornadas a domicilio. En la primera tumbó al Zamora en Vista Alegre (72-57), en la segunda cedió en Palencia dando la talla ante uno de los mejores equipos de la categoría (70-67) y en la tercera cedió en la cancha del sorprendente Bueno Arenas Albacete (81-71).

De los tres resultados, solo el último se sale a priori del guion. Es pronto para delimitar un patrón de conducta de los equipos, con apenas tres jornadas disputadas, pero ahí van tres datos que quizá puedan dar alguna pista: el Coto Córdoba anota tan poco (70 puntos de media) como concede en su aro (69 de promedio) y en el único partido que ganó, contra el Zamora, lo hizo anotando más triples que canastas de dos. Flaquea en el tiro libre (58%) y, aunque dispone de algunos buenos tiradores perimetrales, por ahora no han calibrado bien sus mirillas (33%).

Las amenazas del Coto Córdoba

Mike Nuga y Alejandro Rodríguez, con 18,3 y 11 puntos respectivamente, son los máximos realizadores de un Coto Córdoba que se orquesta también en torno a la picadura del eléctrico Jalen Cone, el talento interior de Pau Treviño y la experiencia del pívot kosovar Mladen Armus, que caza 7,7 rebotes por encuentro. Son los principales activos de un equipo que, a semejanza del sevillano, sabe perfectamente qué importancia tiene blindarse en su cancha para que la temporada no se convierta en un martirio. Rara vez algún equipo que ha luchado y conseguido la permanencia la ha obrado ganando más veces a domicilio que en su pista.

La mejor versión califal debe esperar el Caja 87, al que ante un adversario de parecido rango se le presenta una oportunidad magnífica para aplicar la misma receta de los dos partidos jugados y ganados en San Pablo. No es lo mismo competir en casa que fuera, pero la cercanía del desplazamiento posibilitará que la presencia de aficionados verdirrojos en el pabellón cordobés sea generosa.

Aliento de su gente, siempre presente, tendrá el Caja 87, que en sus dos primeras comparecencias en su feudo se ha mostrado como un equipo reconocible y competitivo que ha crecido en torno a su defensa y se ha sobrepuesto a una baja como la de Moody, jugador capital, en cuya ausencia se podía haber perfectamente justificado si hubiera patinado contra el Palmer Basket o el Partizán de Fuenlabrada. En lugar de ello, Juani Díez reordenó la rotación exprimiendo la versatilidad de sus exteriores para amortiguar los efectos de tan destacada pérdida.

Cierto es que en ambos partidos sufrió alguna que otra desconexión, pero la virtud del Caja 87 fue volver siempre y recuperar el terreno perdido. Contra el Fuenlabrada se marchó seis arriba al intermedio y, aun perdiendo los dos últimos parciales, amarró el partido. Eso es espíritu de lucha, unión y capacidad de resistencia. Cualidades del valor del oro molido que los sevillanos deben seguir trabajando para fusionarlas como señas de identidad. Del doble turno en casa no solo salió indemne el Caja 87, sino feliz y reforzado en unas convicciones que deben guiarlo también a domicilio. Si en Córdoba defiende con la misma intensidad y rigurosidad de las dos últimas jornadas, o del partido de la Copa Andalucía, no es que tenga la victoria hecha, pero sí reunirá méritos para disputarla en un igualado final.

La Copa de España, el torneo por fase de grupos y eliminatorias que organiza la Federación Española de Baloncesto entre los equipos de Primera y Segunda FEB, ya tiene definido su cuadro de octavos de final. Y ahí, entre los 16 mejores conjuntos, se encuentran ... los dos sevillanos, el Insolac Caja 87 y el CB Starlabs Morón, que superaron esta semana al Sol Gironès Bisbal Bàsquet y al Fibwi Palma, respectivamente, en la ronda de dieciseisavos. Los cajistas vencieron por 61-76 en tierras catalanas y los aruncitanos, de Segunda FEB, dieron la sorpresa al tumbar en el pabellón Alameda al equipo balear, de superior categoría (83-74).

En la siguiente fase, los octavos de final, que también se disputarán a un solo partido (igual sucederá en cuartos, semifinales y final), el Caja 87 visitará al UEMC Valladolid, de Segunda FEB; y el Morón volverá a jugar en casa recibiendo al que posiblemente sea el favorito de la Copa de España: el Cajasiete Gran Canaria.

Por potencial de plantilla debería estar peleando por el ascenso directo a la ACB hasta el final. Enfrentarse a un equipo de esta envergadura es ya todo un premio para el CB Morón, que se hace fuerte en su cancha y, en caso de superar esta eliminatoria, se jugaría el pase a la Final Four con el vencedor del Ourense Baloncesto - Palmer Basket Mallorca.

Con un ejercicio serio y profesional aunque discreto en términos anotadores, el Insolac Caja 87 sigue adelante en la Copa de España, donde no hay margen de error al disputarse las eliminatorias a un solo partido hasta la Final Four. Contra el Sol Gironès ... Bisbal Bàsquet de Gerona, en dieciseisavos, el equipo sevillano jugó a rachas y condicionado por su pésimo día en el lanzamiento exterior, firmando apenas 4 triples de 27 intentos. Moody se fue de vacío, con el casillero de puntos a cero, y solo acertaron tres jugadores desde el perímetro: Mendikote, Varela y Cecilia.

Ragsdale, el artillero del conjunto catalán, se disparó hasta los 20 puntos en el primer tiempo, pero en el segundo ajustó la defensa sobre él el Caja 87 y ya no sumó más. No sufrieron los hispalenses, aunque mediado el tercer cuarto permitieron la reacción de un animoso Bisbal Bàsquet que terminó sucumbiendo ante un rival superior y liderado por una luminosa actuación del capitán Dedovic, autor de 20 puntos, 5 rebotes y 3 asistencias (27 de valoración). En octavos, el Caja 87 visitará Pisuerga para enfrentarse al UEMC Valladolid, de Segunda FEB, que dio la sorpresa al superar al Partizán de Fuenlabrada (90-82).

El partido del Caja 87 tuvo más ritmo que puntos desde su explosivo arranque. Un mate con adicional de Leeroy Odiahi y dos triples de Ragsdale le dieron las primeras ventajas al Sil Gironés (9-6) en un duelo que rompió en correcalles. Intentó defender muy agresivo el Caja 87, pero no recuperó una sola pelota y el conjunto catalán arrancó de lo más entonado en el tiro. Bolavie se fue al banco con dos faltas de pardillo en poco más de tres minutos. Latorre, mate a dos manos, elevaba al 11-13, pero el partido, de ataques eléctricos, estaba desencadenado, nadie ponía pausa, al Caja 87 los triples se los repelía el aro y así era imposible que tomara ventajas.

Huérfano de tiro exterior, los sevillanos apretaron más en sus dominios para romper el ritmo anotador de un Bisbal Bàsquet con chispa, bastante afinado, y al que le interesaba mucho más un partido de ida y vuelta que uno de mayor componente físico. Con un quinteto más defensivo, el Caja 87 amplió al 13-17, pero el Bisbal lo equilibró de inmediato antes de que Ramón Vilà se indignara con los árbitros después de ser castigado con falta en ataque tras ser claramente agarrado por un defensor. Soumbey-Alley, con una canasta a tabla tras infiltrarse bajo aro en la retaguardia enemiga, dejaba el 17-19 al término del primer cuarto.

Webster, que no había participado hasta entonces, asumió el timón del Caja 87 en el segundo parcial ante un Sol Gironès que perdía gas a medida que Shad Thomas absorbía juego, tiros y acumulaba fallos, uno tras otro. Los errores los rentabilizó al máximo el Caja 87 para desencadenarse, correr y canjear canastas fáciles, en transición. Ya tenía un colchoncito para dominar y estar más tranquilo. Un 0-6 de parcial justificó el tiempo muerto del cuadro gerundense (17-25).

Ragsdale, desatado

Tampoco Moody, en su regreso a pista, rompió el maleficio cajista desde el triple en dos lanzamientos liberados y cómodos. No era la noche. Sin orden ni acierto en su juego, pura anarquía, el Caja 87 estaba perdonando a su rival. Afortunadamente, en defensa no dejó de trabajar y también cerró el rebote ante un rival cegado en el tiro al que le costaba la vida anotar una canasta. Dedovic subía el 18-27; Latorre, el 21-29; y Dedovic, tras pase de Webster, canasta y bandeja en extensión con adicional, el 21-32. A cuatro minutos, una renta cómoda al fin y perímetro nuevo con Franch, Nacho Varela y Franch, tres manejadores en busca de más control.

Ragsdale, que llevaba 15 puntos, encadenó entonces siete seguidos y taladró el 25-32. Estaba inspiradísimo el escolta norteamericano, desatado, pero también mal defendido. Webster no daba una a derechas, Nacho Varela estaba pasando de puntillas por el partido y Franch sí descifró las defensas rivales para anotar o asistir a sus compañeros. A falta de un minuto para el receso, nuevo tiempo muerto con 30-37 y 20 puntos ya del talentoso Ragsdale. Al intermedio, 32-40 con el segundo triple de los verdirrojos (2/14), ambos anotados por Mendikote.

Ajustando la defensa sobre el bullicioso Ragsdale, el Caja 87 tendría mucho ganado. Obvio. Con 34-44, Dedovic anotaba tras reverso y de inmediato robaba bajo canasta, tras error grosero en el saque de fondo del Bisbal Bàsquet, para colocar el 34-48, máxima renta verdirroja. Rafa García y Soumbey-Alley estaban a los mandos y duraron cinco minutos hasta ser relevados por Nacho Varela y Moody. Bolavie alternaba error con acierto y se colocaba al límite de la eliminación, con cuatro faltas, mientras Sagna, una lapa en defensa, crecía en el partido.

Ni desde el bloqueo directo para jugar el pick&roll ni a través de los indirectos generaba nada el Caja 87, que estaba en bonus en defensa y encajó un 9-0, tras mate de Shad Thomas (43-48). Latorre, en una acción bajo tablero, sufrió un corte en el rostro que lo sacó del partido en plena desconexión de su equipo, que se cortocircuitó y aflojó en defensa cuando dejó de sumar canastas. El tiempo muerto de Juani Díez estaba más que justificado. Dedovic ejerció entonces de capitán, leyó bien las defensas, las superioridades y sumó cuatro puntos que, unidos a una gran canasta de Webster, restablecían el orden. Tras fallo increíble de Shad Thomas, Dedovic devolvía el 9-0 y cerraba el penúltimo cuarto (43-57).

Última rebelión local

No se rindió aún el Bisbal, que arrancó el último con toda la cuerda dada y un 8-3 (51-60), con ataques rápidos y certeros aprovechando una laxitud defensiva del Caja 87 que a Juani Díez no le gustó un pelo. Que se complicara el partido, con siete minutos por delante, era realmente improbable, pero se trataba de ganar haciéndolo con cierta solvencia y finalizando con buenas sensaciones. En estos partidos importa sobre todo el qué, pero las formas ayudan también a crecer como colectivo. El Caja 87 de las dos caras que arrancó con la brújula perdida ante el Palmer Basket y acabó con las máximas revoluciones defensivas, en base a un patrón de juego que le ha dado resultado hasta la fecha, tiene que crecer hacia el ... de esa segunda parte. Blindado en los dominios de su canasta, el equipo se apretó las tuercas y lo hizo activándose de piernas y manos, jugando con mucho más deseo. Así consiguió cuatro objetivos: ser más reconocible, cortocircuitar a su rival, conectar con la grada y apoderarse de su primer triunfo en la Primera FEB. Una victoria histórica de la que ya toca pasar página, sin olvidar las enseñanzas que dejó para ponerlas de nuevo en práctica, porque ya es su deber dirigir el foco a la tercera jornada y a la visita a San Pablo de un rival de armas tomar.

Quizá no sea de la primerísima línea en las quinielas por el ascenso, pero el equipo que aparece este domingo por Sevilla es un clásico del baloncesto español que merece todo el respeto y precisará la mejor versión del Caja 87. Con el casillero de victorias sin estrenar, a cero, llega el Partizán de Fuenlabrada (12.30, Baloncesto TV, con arbitraje de Zafra Guerra, Marqueta Gracia, Olmo Ochoa).

Los fuenlabreños han tomado el nombre del emblemático club de Belgrado como muestra de la alianza de colaboración alcanzada por ambas entidades, que mantienen una buena e histórica relación desde que los serbios, por la Guerra de los Balcanes, se movieran a Fuenlabrada para disputar sus partidos. Un hermanamiento de 35 años que se ha materializado en un proyecto común y se ha reflejado también en la adopción de esa nueva denominación por parte del equipo español.

Por una razón similar a lo que le sucede al Estudiantes y, ahora también al Gran Canaria, mientras el Fuenlabrada se encuentre en Primera FEB hay que otorgarle la etiqueta de candidato al ascenso. Es más, el hecho de que no haya empezado bien, pleno de derrotas suma en las dos primeras jornadas, es un motivo de peso para que el Caja 87 active al máximo sus niveles de alerta. Porque un rival de ese potencial se vuelve aún más peligroso en la necesidad, cuando anda herido. Y el Fuenlabrada seguro que lo está. En la primera jornada cayó a domicilio con el Lucentum Alicante (96-82), que apunta alto esta temporada; y en la segunda, se vio superado en el Fernando Martín por el Gran Canaria (79-68).

Tras esos dos reveses, el Fuenlabrada quiere borrar ese incómodo cero de su casilla de triunfos y tratará de hacerlo en San Pablo. Sin una rotación demasiado larga, tiene elementos de muchos quilates en su roster, como el brasileño Vítor Benite, que sigue impartiendo magisterio a los 36 años tras una larguísima y fructífera carrera en el baloncesto español. Un tipo querido y respetado que dejó huella en los meses que estuvo en Sevilla, liderando a un Betis Baloncesto que ascendió deportivamente de categoría antes del final ya conocido por todos.

Los otros conocidos

También vistió de verdiblanco Iván Cruz hace unos años e Iñaki Martín, que estuvo entre los candidatos este verano al banquillo del Caja 87, ejerció de asistente de Bruno Savignani en Sevilla hace tres temporadas. Pero hay más en el arsenal del Fuenlabrada: de Mateo Díaz en la dirección a la calidad en el perímetro de Jonathan Zhao, ex del CB Zaragoza; y el músculo de Prince Ali, Belemene o Cardoso; sin olvidar la altura y capacidad intimidatoria de Goran Huskic.

Dispone el Fuenlabrada de todos esos ingredientes para poner en aprietos a cualquiera. Entre otros, al Caja 87, que debe andarse con ojo, entender la jerarquía de su rival desde el salto inicial y elevar al máximo su nivel físico porque el partido lo requerirá. Siempre no podrá enmendar la plana en 20 minutos y corregirse a tiempo como le sucedió ante el Palmer Basket. El Fuenlabrada está a la altura competitiva, o muy cerquita, del Estudiantes y el Gran Canaria. Y contra rivales de esta envergadura no se permiten las desconexiones profundas ni los partidos a dos velocidades. Entendiendo que es imposible mantener los 40 minutos el nivel de desgaste defensivo de la segunda parte contra el Palmer, el Caja 87 ya sabe cuál es el camino donde hallará el éxito. Es decir, qué claves del pentagrama ha de tocar con mimo y delicadeza para acercarse a la sinfonía de la victoria.

Debe apostar por el sacrificio defensivo jugando a gran intensidad y con ayudas, bloqueando caminos y anticipándose a los pases adversarios, siendo agresivo en la primera línea y también sólido en el rebote. Siempre es mucho más fácil escribirlo que ejecutarlo. Pero el equipo de Juani Díez puede hacerlo y debe moverse en registros anotadores más bien modestos, en la horquilla de los 75-80 puntos. Superada esa cota, lo normal es que sus opciones mengüen ante un equipo como el Fuenlabrada, pero esto no deja de ser un apriorismo que el baloncesto, la verdad de la cancha, puede dejar en papel mojado.

Muy al contrario, se vislumbraba un partido igualado, de extremo sufrimiento, por el peso en la categoría de un Menorca con elementos de nivel en su plantilla que la pasada temporada se había metido en el play off y en la presente no da una a derechas. Con pleno de derrotas tras cinco jornadas celebradas, la comparecencia del Caja 87 estaba marcada en rojo para los de Javier Zamora, que sufrieron la baja de última hora de uno de sus mejores jugadores, el exverdiblanco Cvetkovic.

Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5: the cheapest, fastest, and most capable small model we’ve ever released.

Claude Haiku 5.5 is designed for high-volume, cost-sensitive tasks. It reliably handles quick and repetitive workloads (like summaries, compactions, database queries, and classification requests). It pairs well with Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 as a subagent on coding work. And, since it’s also our fastest model to date, it works especially well for speed-sensitive tasks like live customer support and browser use.¹

Haiku 5.5 is available at a much lower price than Haiku 4.5. On average, it now costs around 75% less to run.²

Along with this launch, we’re making improvements to the value of our model range. We’re halving the price of Claude Sonnet 5.5’s cache reads, which means Sonnet 5.5 now runs around 20% cheaper on most agentic work. And we’re introducing a new monthly API credit for our Claude Max, Ultra, and Team subscribers, designed to support our users in building new agents and applications that run on the Claude Platform.

Safety

Alignment. Claude Haiku 5.5 shows major improvements across almost all of our alignment evaluations relative to Haiku 4.5. In particular, we found far fewer instances of misaligned behavior, and a lower willingness to cooperate with misuse. The model’s system card describes our evaluation process and results in more detail.

Safeguards. Consistent with its capabilities, Haiku 5.5’s cybersecurity safeguards are more restrictive than Haiku 4.5’s, but somewhat less restrictive than those we’ve applied to other recent models. In cybersecurity, they permit a wider range of defensive tasks than our safeguards for Sonnet 5.5, but they still block penetration testing and other techniques more likely to be used by attackers.

Haiku 5.5’s biology safeguards are the same as for Sonnet 5, Sonnet 5.5, and Opus 5. They allow research biology questions but restrict access to requests that we judge as likely to cause harm. Organizations working on wider-ranging biology and cyber activities can apply to our Life Sciences Verification Program and Cyber Verification Program.

Availability

Claude Haiku 5.5 is available now on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. On the Claude Platform, developers can get started with claude-haiku-5-5.

See our migration guide for details.

Further updates

Alongside our new pricing for Claude Haiku 5.5, we’re making further improvements to the value of our models and products.

First, starting today, we’re lowering the price of cache reads on Claude Sonnet 5.5. Cache reads now cost 50% less: $0.10 per million tokens rather than $0.20. Because cache reads make up a large share of models’ token consumption, this reduces the cost of Sonnet 5.5 on most agentic tasks by around 20%.

For instance, here’s what the price cut means for Sonnet 5.5’s performance relative to cost on Terminal-Bench 4.0:

Terminal-Bench 4.0 measures how well a model can complete complex, multi-step professional tasks within a command-line interface.

This chart illustrates an important difference between Haiku 5.5 and our larger models. Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 remain better choices for complex agentic coding tasks like those measured by Terminal-Bench 4.0. By contrast, Haiku 5.5 is best suited to more narrowly scoped tasks that might otherwise have been cost-prohibitive with previous versions of Claude—like compaction, summarization, or subagent work.

Second, this week, we’ll roll out a new monthly API credit to all Max, Ultra, and Team subscribers for use on the Claude Platform. Max users will get $100 in credits per month, Ultra users will get $200, and Team subscribers will receive up to $500, pooled across their users. These credits are designed to allow our users to experiment with building tools, apps, and agents that call our API. They can be used on any of our models. For more information, see our Help Center article.

For developers, we’re also updating our Claude Python and TypeScript SDKs to add support for computer use and browser use in beta. Haiku 5.5 is especially well-suited to these tasks, given its combination of speed, capability, and price. You can read more about this in our Claude Platform docs.

We’re introducing Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in our new Claude 5.5 family. It performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work and costs 40% less to run than Opus 5.

Claude Opus 5.5 is our first release since we called for pacing the frontier. It was tested before release by external evaluators, including Frontier Design and METR. On our automated behavioral audit, the most comprehensive alignment test we run, Opus 5.5 is the strongest-performing model we’ve tested to date. It also comes with the safeguards we’ve developed for our most capable models.

Here are some of the improvements you can expect from Opus 5.5:

Performance. Opus 5.5 is a major step up from Opus 5. It’s the new leading model, and early testers saw large jumps in performance on their most complex work. One tester completed a 680,000-line code migration in less than a day—work that would have taken an engineering team weeks. It’s good at finding and fixing inefficiencies in software: when we asked it to cut load times across every page of a web app, Opus 5.5 succeeded 39 of 40 times, while Opus 5 made smaller improvements that also altered the app’s behavior. A different tester had several Claude models build a game from a single prompt; Opus 5.5 scored higher than any other model on the strength of its graphics and polish.

Safety. Opus 5.5 achieves the best scores of any model to date on our automated behavioral audit, our alignment suite that tests Claude across thousands of simulated scenarios. It is much less likely than recent models to take hard-to-reverse actions or act outside the boundaries it’s been given, and it’s more resistant than Opus 5 to prompt injection. We’ve also broadened our alignment testing to cover longer tasks, impossible tasks, and scenarios modeled on real incidents, though it still has limits. Full details of our evaluation are available in the Opus 5.5 System Card.

Because Opus 5.5 is comparable to Claude Mythos 5.1 in biology and cybersecurity, we’re deploying it with safeguards similar to those on Claude Fable 5.1. Vetted organizations can apply today to our Life Sciences Verification Program to use Opus 5.5 for biology research. In the coming weeks we will also be expanding access to our Cyber Verification Program, and verified cybersecurity practitioners will be able to use Opus 5.5 for their work.

Cost and speed. Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that. Our tests show that at default settings it will cost 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads. Input and output tokens are $4 and $20 per million, 20% less than Opus 5. Cache reads (which make up the majority of agentic and coding work costs) are $0.20 per million tokens, 60% less than Opus 5. Safety

Pacing the frontier

Last week, our CEO, Dario Amodei, argued that AI progress should be paced so that safety practices stay ahead of model capabilities. Pacing is an approach to keeping AI safe, remaining competitive with China, and realizing AI’s benefits, particularly in areas like biology and medicine.

We largely understand the risks today’s models present and are well equipped to manage them. However, more serious risks could emerge quickly as capabilities improve, and we need to prepare for them now. For that reason, our safety work takes place on two time horizons at once:

Safety practices for current models. The current generation of models relies on an established set of practices: extensive alignment testing, pre-release evaluation by outside organizations such as METR and Frontier Design, and safeguards matched to each model’s capabilities in high-risk areas like cybersecurity and biology. We refine these practices with each release. We believe they are appropriate to the worst risks today’s models present, and that they give us a broad, though not perfect, picture of the range of serious risks.

Additionally, we track our ability to train and evaluate aligned models, and we report on both our public and internal models in the risk reports we publish under our Responsible Scaling Policy, our voluntary framework for managing catastrophic risks from advanced AI systems.

Preparing for future models. We’re preparing our training and evaluation processes in anticipation of more advanced models. We’re tightening how we filter the environments used in reinforcement learning, since flawed environments are a major source of misaligned behavior. Additionally, we’re improving our alignment rewards and developing automated processes for producing new, diverse scenarios for safety training. And we are strengthening our security and monitoring, including a focused effort to improve interpretability-based monitoring and evaluation. We hope such techniques will help reduce our reliance on auditing a model’s chain-of-thought, or the reasoning it writes out while it works.

Models with greater capabilities—such as those that can fully automate the work of AI research itself—require a higher safety standard still. Our calls for pacing were based in large part on our expectation that such models could be trained soon. For these models, we do not assume the measures described above will meet that safety standard on their own. As AI becomes more capable, public policy should play a larger role in making sure the systems people rely on are safe. That capacity takes time to build, and we’ve started to put the infrastructure in place to support it, as described in “We Must Pace the Frontier” and our recent announcement with Accenture; we expect to share more details on these efforts soon. We will also continue to contribute to policy discussions with government and industry, including on approaches to regulation and international coordination.

Alignment

On our primary evaluation suite, an automated behavioral audit that assesses Claude across nearly 2,000 scenarios, Opus 5.5 scored better than any recent Claude model on nearly every measure of misaligned behavior. It’s also our strongest model on most measures of honesty.

In particular, Opus 5.5 improves over previous models on several of the behaviors that contributed to recent cybersecurity incidents, including biased or motivated reasoning, attempting to escape a sandbox, and taking harmful actions after concluding it was in a simulated environment. In a new evaluation designed to test a model’s propensity to cross containment boundaries, Opus 5.5 attempted to circumvent boundaries around 85% less often than Opus 5 or Claude Mythos 5.1, and every attempt it made was low severity and self-reported. For teams running Claude unattended across their codebases and systems, this is just as important as raw capability.

However, as we described in our recent alignment assessment, building evaluations that reliably catch every failure prior to deployment remains an unsolved problem. We see signs that Opus 5.5 often suspects it is being evaluated, which challenges our ability to assess how it will act in the vast variety of real-world settings it is deployed in. As these settings expand and model capabilities increase, we expect this challenge to grow, unless we make progress on interpretability. Although we are confident that Opus 5.5 shows broad improvements in the areas we are able to measure, we pair our own alignment work with the safeguards described below.

Safeguards

As our models grow more powerful, stricter safeguards are one way we prevent new capabilities from becoming tools for misuse. Opus 5.5 is the first Opus model to launch with a similar class of safeguards to Fable 5.1 on cybersecurity, biology, and distillation, all of which fall back to another model transparently.

Cybersecurity. Because Opus 5.5 has extremely strong cyber capabilities, we’re applying cybersecurity safeguards to Opus 5.5 that are similar to Fable 5.1’s. Users will be able to identify and fix bugs in their code as part of the routine software development lifecycle, but most cybersecurity tasks will be re-routed to Opus 4.8.

For cyberdefenders, we’ll soon be expanding our Cyber Verification Program to include Opus 5.5. The new program will include three tiers for increasingly permissive trusted access, including access to Claude Mythos models. Claude Security is already available with access to Claude Mythos 5.1.

Biology. Opus 5.5 is highly capable in biology, exceeding Opus 5 and matching or beating Claude Mythos 5.1 across many areas of work. For example, Opus 5.5 achieved improvements on a long-horizon molecular prediction and design evaluation conducted in collaboration with Dyno Therapeutics, and expert red-teamers rated its scientific novelty as comparable to the best model they had tested.

For this reason, Opus 5.5 uses the same biology safeguards as Fable 5.1. To use Opus 5.5 for research and development work impeded by these safeguards, users can apply to our new Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted organizations like academic labs, startups, and pharmaceutical companies access to safeguards designed for the full breadth of biology-related work. Interested organizations can apply here.

Distillation

Distillation attacks, in which attackers use thousands of fake accounts to extract a model’s capabilities at industrial scale, create safety and national security risks. Distillation allows bad actors to create highly capable models without the safeguards we build into Claude. Our September 2026 threat intelligence report details the illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far.

Opus 5.5 is launching with preserved thinking, the anti-distillation safeguard we introduced with Fable 5.1. It stops API users from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract Claude’s reasoning. It applies to Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 for API accounts created on or after August 31, 2026. Our Help Center article explains the change, and our preserved thinking docs show how to test and update your integrations.

Data retention and compliance

Like previous Opus models, Opus 5.5 is available with zero data retention.

As with Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 comes with our watermarking measures to comply with the EU AI Act, discussed here. It is also no longer available with “thinking” mode switched off, as we describe here.

Sonnet 5.5 is a faster, lower-cost complement to Claude Opus 5.5. Where Opus 5.5 is built for complex work requiring careful judgment, Sonnet 5.5 is strongest at well-scoped everyday tasks, fixing bugs, and creating polished documents, slides, and spreadsheets. Safety

Alignment

Sonnet 5.5 doesn’t advance the frontier of our models’ capabilities, so our alignment assessment focused on a targeted set of risks that apply to models of any capability level, including acting against users’ interests, misleading users, and cooperating with high-stakes misuse.

On our automated behavioral audit, which tests Claude across roughly 1,850 scenarios, Sonnet 5.5 improves on or matches Sonnet 5 on most measures of alignment, resistance to misuse, and honesty. On our newer containment evaluations, Sonnet 5.5 comes close to Opus 5.5, the best model we tested, in how rarely it tries to escape its sandbox, and it’s the least likely of any of our models to probe the limits of its containers. Across the full audit, Opus 5.5 still performs slightly better overall, but we found no evidence that Sonnet 5.5 pursues goals that conflict with the user’s intention.

As we described in our recent alignment assessment, no set of evaluations reliably catches every failure, and Sonnet 5.5 may have tendencies we haven’t found, which is why we pair our own alignment work with the safeguards described below.

Safeguards

Cybersecurity. Sonnet 5.5’s cyber capabilities are a large improvement over Sonnet 5’s, so we’re deploying it with safeguards similar to those on Opus 5.5. Users can still find and fix bugs in their code as part of routine software development, but higher-risk cybersecurity tasks will visibly fall back to Sonnet 5. Soon, cyberdefenders will be able to apply to our expanded Cyber Verification Program for tiered access to more advanced capabilities on Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Claude Mythos models.

Biology. Sonnet 5.5 uses the same set of biology safeguards as Sonnet 5. These target harmful requests; most research, education, and clinical work is unaffected, though some microbiology and virology requests may be flagged in error. Organizations can apply to our Life Sciences Verification Program for access to safeguards designed for the full breadth of biology-related work.

Distillation. Distillation attacks, in which attackers use thousands of fake accounts to extract a model’s capabilities at industrial scale, allow bad actors to create highly capable models without the safeguards we build into Claude. Because Sonnet 5.5 is far more capable than its predecessor, it’s the first Sonnet model to launch with safety classifiers that prevent reasoning extraction. Sonnet 5.5 also expands preserved thinking, so Claude’s thinking cannot be decoupled from the account that created it. Most developers won’t notice a change. If you move conversations between accounts, including switching accounts mid-session in Claude Code, our docs article explains the change.

Getting started

As with Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 is available with zero data retention.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 is now available on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started on the Claude Platform with claude-sonnet-5-5. If you run Sonnet with thinking off, you’ll need to switch to the new between_tools setting, which keeps up-front thinking off, before moving to Sonnet 5.5. See our migration guide for details.

SSince May, teams on the ground in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have been combating a rare strain of Ebolavirus called Bundibugyo (BDBV). Every day, relais communautaires knock on doors of homes, offer counsel, learn of recoveries and deaths, and refer anyone with suspicious symptoms to get care.

In an outbreak like this one, a health worker's notebook is often the first and most complete record of when a person got sick, who they touch, and where they went before they knew they were infected. In the BDBV outbreak, almost half of the nearly 8,000 confirmed cases have died. How quickly someone is found—before their condition turns critical and while they can still be treated—often determines whether they survive.

Once a vaccine becomes available, that same contact information will tell responders exactly where it needs to go. A faster, more accurate picture of who was exposed means people can be found and protected before they ever fall ill. But the speed of this response is limited by how quickly the data can be passed along the chain from the notebooks of health workers, to the labs confirming diagnoses, and to the ministries and funders deciding where resources go next.

Health facilities send case information to their districts, often over WhatsApp, and send biological samples to local labs for sequencing. Each district puts case information onto PowerPoint slides and sends it on to the outbreak coordination center. At the provincial health ministry, the staff compiling the reports work late nights pulling together this information into slide decks. These decks turn into the published situation report, or sitrep.

The creation of sitreps, and the greater outbreak response, has recently started to look different in eastern DRC, thanks to a partnership convened by the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) with, among others, the WHO Regional Office for Africa (WHO AFRO) and the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB). These organizations have been working with Anthropic's Beneficial Deployments and Applied AI teams to use Claude to analyze community health workers’ field data, to systematically monitor and review research evidence, and to use our scientific workbench.

“I have fought this virus for fifty years. The tools have changed completely, but the rule has not: you beat Ebola by knowing where it is today, not where it was last week.”

Dr. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, Director General of DRC’s National Institute of Biomedical Research, special adviser to the director general of the Africa CDC, and co-discoverer of the Ebolavirus in 1976

Saving time and enabling analysis

The emergencies hub of WHO AFRO is headquartered in Dakar, Senegal. The response team handles about a hundred public health events a year, often deploying on missions to affected regions to gather data and work on processes.

Tendai Muza works on data systems and analytics at WHO AFRO. With his colleagues Tamayi Mlanda and Gianni-Ferrari Donkor Muza, he built a Claude skill to accelerate the sitrep process. With the skill, Claude knows to pull the case and lab numbers out of each health zone’s PowerPoint deck, check them against the previous day’s report, flag any change in the trend (and explain what might be going on with it), and then summarize the districts’ reports. A sitrep that used to take all day to put together can now take under an hour.

For the data teams, in addition to streamlining the sitrep process with Claude, they are also using it for analysis and disease modeling. Paul Ouma of the WHO AFRO team said, “Previously we couldn't even start thinking of which disease model might be better. We could only run with one, because of time constraints.” Now they can run multiple models at a time with Claude and build forecasts to help, for example, logistics staff decide where treatment centers should be built.

Connecting global teams on vaccine development

There is currently no approved vaccine for BDBV, but there is a vaccine, Ervebo, for the Zaire strain. When BDBV emerged, CEPI invited proposals to advance potential vaccine candidates and related vaccine science. Polina Brangel, R&D Data Innovation Lead at CEPI told us, "Claude does not decide which cohorts of serological samples should be analyzed to generate evidence on Ervebo's potential cross-reactivity against BDBV — that remains a scientific judgement made by experts.” What Claude currently does is “organize complex, multi-factor data in a way that allows the human eye to compare across a wide range of proposals and draw conclusions within a much shorter timeframe.”

CEPI used Claude to build a dashboard that helped more quickly and robustly track the actions and work needed to be done by teams to advance vaccine development.

“This has been an opportunity to learn, in real time, where AI could make a practical difference for teams working under pressure.”

Polina Brangel, R&D Data Innovation Lead at CEPI

Claude for Science

In outbreak labs—where samples collected by health workers are sequenced to confirm cases and trace how the virus is changing–the bottleneck to results is often the computer analysis of a virus’s genetic data (known as bioinformatics). Reading the virus’s genome can reveal which cases are linked, whether the virus is spreading through chains that haven’t been spotted by case counts, and whether the virus is changing in ways that could undermine tests, treatments or vaccines.

The INRB lab has produced essentially all of the BDBV genomes sequenced from DRC cases in the current outbreak. Each of their sequencing machines produces millions of short fragments of genetic code. Piecing together a virus's full genome from those fragments has traditionally meant typing specialized commands into a programmer's terminal. But Claude Science, an AI workbench for scientists, can be prompted in plain language to assemble the genome and build the virus's family tree. Especially during major outbreaks, bioinformatics capacity is limited, and Claude Science significantly lowers the barrier to produce analysis that can be used to trace new infections. It can also help estimate the scale of the outbreak, and identify new variants.

WHO Africa is already thinking about applying these tools to other outbreaks. For an outbreak of chikungunya—a debilitating disease spread mosquitoes—it is using Claude to clean and validate “line lists” that describe an outbreak by person, place, and time. This is work that would have taken much longer without AI.

Next, the WHO team wants to use Claude to stitch together historical disease databases, so that decisions in the next outbreak can draw on the last ones. In the past, this has been too time consuming to do in the midst of a crisis.

The future of outbreak response

Global health partners are beginning to understand how AI tools can bring the greatest benefit during an outbreak. The Bundibugyo Ebola response still has a long way to go. Containing it will take time–although there are some promising signs of the outbreak slowing in Ituri. Response teams are helping the world learn what responsible, practical AI deployment can look like in real-world public health situations, where time is of the essence.
